title: Praying for the dead
hook: the living pray for the dead, and the Qur'an is recited for them in many communities

segments.voice: Yesterday, what continues: ongoing charity, knowledge that benefits, and a child who prays. Your line: three things continue. Which one did you choose? Today, the third door, opened wide. Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

A man came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a worry about his mother. It's in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'A'ishah. His mother had died suddenly, he said, and he thought that if she'd had the chance to speak, she would have given something in charity. So: if I give charity for her now, will it reach her? The Prophet said yes. A son, too late for one last conversation, asking if there's still a way to do something for her. And being told there is.
screen: `HIS MOTHER DIED SUDDENLY.` → `WILL IT REACH HER?` → `YES.`

segments.voice: That yes is the floor this whole day stands on: in Islam, the living can still do something for the dead. And the first thing, the one anyone can do, is du'a, a personal prayer asking God for them. The Qur'an itself gives words for it. In surah Ibrahim, the prophet Abraham prays, in Pickthall's translation: "Our Lord! Forgive me and my parents and believers on the day when the account is cast." And in surah al-Hashr, those who came later in the faith say: "Our Lord! Forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith." Look at who's in those prayers. Me, my parents, the believers, the ones who went before. The prayer doesn't pick one person out of the line. It holds the whole line at once. The funeral prayer you met earlier is itself a du'a for the one who died. The greeting at the graves asks well-being for the dead. And yesterday's hadith counts a child's prayer among the things that keep reaching a person after death. Then there's the Qur'an recited for the dead. In some communities, people gather after a death to recite, and some read surah Ya Sin. Here the scholars have differed. Some hold that the reward of recitation can be given to the dead and reaches them. Others hold to what the hadith name directly, such as du'a and charity, and are cautious about more. Both views draw on the texts, and on love for the dead. And the plainest part is shared by both: remember them, and ask God for them.
screen: `WILL IT REACH HER? YES.` · `DU'A: ASKING GOD FOR THEM.` · `ME, MY PARENTS, THE BELIEVERS.` · `RECITATION: THE SCHOLARS DIFFER.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for someone who died, or, if you don't pray, remember them with care. Settle and breathe. Let one person come to mind: a grandparent, a friend, someone you never quite said goodbye to. Say their name, quietly. Remember one specific thing about them: a laugh, a phrase, a meal. If you pray, you can use Abraham's words from surah Ibrahim: Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers. Or the words from al-Hashr, for those who were before us. Stay with them a while. The bell holds the time.
Praying for the dead. Du'a and charity offered for those who have died, which the hadith says can still reach them. Today's word.
Your line: remember them in du'a. Today, at a pause, say one person's name who has died, and add a prayer or a good wish for them. Tomorrow, writing a will. Day one thousand three hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims make du'a for their dead, using words like those in Qur'an 14:41 and 59:10, and give charity in their names; in some communities people also gather to recite the Qur'an, sometimes surah Ya Sin, though scholars differ on whether the reward of recitation reaches the dead.
